html:
Stockfish is cod dried on wooden racks in the cold wind of northern Norway, especially in the Lofoten islands. It was Norway's chief export for most of a thousand years.

Every winter the cod come to spawn off Lofoten. Dried without salt, the fish keeps for years and travels well. From the 1100s stockfish went south to Bergen and from there across Europe, where Catholics ate it on fast days. In Italy it became baccalà, and in Portugal salted cod became bacalhau.

The trade paid for grain imports and for Bergen's wealth, and shaped settlement along the north coast. Racks of drying fish are still a common sight in Lofoten. Much of it now goes to Nigeria, a trade that began in the Biafran war. See Norway.
